title: Leaving Arab lands
hookLine: Jewish families leave, or are forced out of, Middle Eastern and North African countries

lines: A PHOTOGRAPH ON A KITCHEN SHELF.
A CITY THEY CAN'T GO BACK TO.
cards: A black-and-white photograph sits in a frame on a kitchen shelf: a synagogue courtyard, a few men in suits, a boy squinting into the sun.
The family who owns it can tell you the city, Baghdad, and the street, and the name of the boy, now somebody's grandfather. They can't take you there.
Families from Cairo, Aleppo, Tripoli, Fez and Sana'a keep photographs like this, and recipes, and songs. They were Jewish families who lived among Arab and Muslim neighbors for generations.
Then, from the years around the founding of Israel onward, they left, or were pushed out.

teach.h: SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.
teach.b: Jewish life in these lands was old.

Tradition says the Jews of Iraq go back to the exile in Babylon, when the prophet Jeremiah wrote to the captives: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it."
Families did that, generation after generation, as merchants, doctors, musicians, rabbis. There were good years and hard years under different rulers.
Then, as the conflict over the land of Israel grew, the ground shifted under them.
The details differ from country to country. In some places there were riots and killings. In some, Jews lost their jobs, their property or their citizenship.
In some, families slipped out quietly; in others, they were allowed to go only if they left nearly everything behind. Some went to France, Britain or the Americas.
Others went to the new State of Israel, arriving with very little. And some Muslim neighbors helped: they hid a family, kept a shop safe, said goodbye in tears. Those stories are told too.
Jews from these lands are often called Mizrahi, a Hebrew word meaning eastern.

teach.h: KEPT ALIVE IN SONGS AND SPICES.
teach.b: Families kept the old places alive anyway: in Judeo-Arabic songs, in a grandmother's spices, in the way a cousin still says the name of a street in Cairo. Yesterday's line was nowhere to go.
Today's adds a piece to the same map: they left too. Saying it takes nothing from anyone else's loss. Two griefs can sit at one table, as two memories of one year did a few days ago.

how: Mizrahi and Sephardi families often keep the memory of the cities they left through food, liturgical melodies and family stories, and some hold gatherings to record the histories of the cities they left.

games.q: you are a Jewish family in an old city where your great-grandparents lived. after years of growing danger, you are told you may leave, but only with what you can carry. what do you do?
o: stay, and hope things calm down.
pack what you can carry and go.
try to sell everything first, then leave slowly.
games.why: in the stories families tell, they packed what they could carry and left, some to Israel, some to Europe or the Americas. almost everything else stayed behind.

practice: If your own family has a story of leaving, from any country, bring it to mind: who packed, what they carried, what stayed behind.

If you don't know one, picture someone you could ask, a grandparent, a coworker, a neighbor, and imagine asking them gently where their family's table used to be. Hold that story the way you'd hold an old photograph, by the edges.
